questions.prompt: Which mental model best explains “Understanding Compiled CSS” in Dart Sass?
options: The best solution is always to replace native CSS behavior with a new Sass abstraction.

Sass extends CSS with a compile-time layer for reusable values, expressions, rules, and module organization. The compiler transforms the source file into ordinary CSS; the browser does not execute Sass syntax.
The browser executes Sass source directly, so a compilation step is unnecessary.
Readable SCSS guarantees correct browser rendering, accessibility, and performance without output review.
questions.answer_key: Sass extends CSS with a compile-time layer for reusable values, expressions, rules, and module organization. The compiler transforms the source file into ordinary CSS; the browser does not execute Sass syntax.
questions.explanation: Sass extends CSS with a compile-time layer for reusable values, expressions, rules, and module organization. The compiler transforms the source file into ordinary CSS; the browser does not execute Sass syntax. The alternative choices confuse Sass compilation with browser execution or claim guarantees that require independent tests.

questions.prompt: When applying “Sass-to-CSS transformation”, which approach is the most reliable?
options: Reproduce the issue with the smallest entrypoint, read the first relevant diagnostic, fix the source rather than the generated file, and recompile to verify the correction.
Skip compilation and infer the final selector list and property values from the source file alone.
Prefer deeply nested selectors because fewer source lines always mean simpler and safer CSS.
Silence every warning before determining whether it identifies a deprecated or incorrect construct.
questions.answer_key: Reproduce the issue with the smallest entrypoint, read the first relevant diagnostic, fix the source rather than the generated file, and recompile to verify the correction.
questions.explanation: Reproduce the issue with the smallest entrypoint, read the first relevant diagnostic, fix the source rather than the generated file, and recompile to verify the correction. Compare the compiled output with the stated intent and preserve browser-native behavior where it is required.

questions.prompt: Which review decision most directly supports maintainability for “Understanding Compiled CSS”?
options: Generate every possible selector or theme combination, even when most variants are never used.
Treat successful compilation as proof that the interface is accessible and behaves correctly in every browser.
Expose internal implementation details as public API and postpone documentation until after release.

Start with a small example, state the expected CSS behavior, compile it with Dart Sass, and compare the output with the intent. Retain the plain-CSS alternative when Sass adds no meaningful reuse or organization.
